title: When a Carpenter Restores a Camaro, Every Detail Is Accounted For

body_markdown:
I’ve seen a lot of cars in nearly eight decades on this planet, but few impressed me at first glance the way Frank Young’s Camaro did. This isn’t the kind of car that shouts “look at me,” like a bright red machine with an abundance of chrome and a blower sticking out of the hood might do. With clean, sleek lines, minimal brightwork, and dressed in shades of grey, it’s the kind of car that seductively whispers sweet nothings in your ear. Smitten, I asked Young to tell me about his car and how it came to be.


The exquisite detail and superb craftsmanship evident in the build of his ’69 Camaro Z28 restomod is, to a great extent, the result of many years spent building custom homes. Like many Michigan youngsters, Young was into automobiles from an early age, but his skill set was largely developed as a home-building contractor and finishing carpenter.


“I got my start in home construction on a roughing crew many years ago,” Young said. “Those are the guys who frame the house, and if they don’t get it right, the building will be subpar. You learn to do things correctly.” Young later moved on to a supervisory role, overseeing every element of home construction. “These were high-end custom homes for professionals,” he added. “They had to be flawless.” When all the plumbing, electrical, and other mechanical work had been completed to Young’s satisfaction, he put on his tool belt and went to work as the finishing carpenter. His wrap-up role was to make the home a treat for the eyes. “What the finishing carpenter does includes all the important details. It’s what everyone sees,” he said.


In profile, the uncluttered flanks and smooth lines of Young’s Z28 offer a fresh interpretation of what this iconic machine can be.


Paul Stenquist


The Z28 badging in the grille was retained. Note the snug fit of the body-color bumper. That flush, hardware-free look was made possible by welding mounting brackets to the inside of the bumper.


Paul Stenquist


Kindig-It Design door handles mount flush. They lock and unlock via a remote control.


Paul Stenquist


Young found the classic Z28 striping too loud for his subtle styling approach, so a patterned stripe in a slightly darker grey was sprayed over the finish.


Paul Stenquist


Front and rear bumpers were stripped of chrome and shortened so they wrap snugly around the sides of the body.


Paul Stenquist


Today, Young is, for the most part, retired from the construction business, but he keeps busy running a well-equipped auto restoration shop in Fort Gratiot, Michigan. His childhood friend, Jim Fraser, works with him almost every day. Young and Fraser played hockey together as kids and have remained lifelong buddies through nearly 70 years. Fraser’s Firebird, which was built in Young’s shop,[was previously featured on this site](https://www.hagerty.com/media/car-profiles/from-commuter-to-restomod-this-71-firebird-has-the-right-formula/) .


How Young’s experience building luxury homes for fussy customers translated to building a beautiful automobile is evident in the fine detail and exquisite lines of his Camaro. He bought the car seven years ago, as a very nice, restored car, and was not quite sure what he was going to do with it. “I had considered leaving it as is, driving it and enjoying it, but I eventually decided it didn’t meet my standards,” Young said.


The frame connectors are bolted to the front subframe and buried within the unibody structure. Young designed the exhaust system and welded it up with 2.5-inch tubing.


Erik Stenquist


He tore the car down to the studs, as they say in the construction biz, and sold most of the pieces. “My friends gave me hell for parting out the car,“ he recalled. “But it wasn’t the car I wanted.” He retained little more than some of the sheetmetal, and even there he found it necessary to clean things up. For example, rusty areas in the floor had been repaired with patches. Young cut out the entire interior and trunk floors and replaced them.


He wanted a smooth, seamless look, so he removed the bumpers, stripped them of chrome, cut them in half, and rewelded them so that they would hug the sides of the body. To bring the bumpers in tight, front and rear, he welded mounting brackets to the inside of the bumpers, eliminating mounting hardware and enabling a flush fit.


The rear window is flush-mounted, as is the rear bumper, and the tailpipes are tucked up into the body. That kind of attention to detail makes this car special.


Paul Stenquist


Hunkered down over big rubber, this sleek Camaro is ready to pounce.


Paul Stenquist


Young ordered oversize glass for the windshield and rear window, then mounted them seamlessly, without the chrome trim that hides the body/window joints on the factory build. The two pieces of glass needed for this modification set him back $1400. The side light markers were eliminated front and rear, as were the door handles and locks. In their place are flush-mounted handles and locks. To open the doors, you push in on one end of the handle and pull out on the other. Young does it effortlessly with one hand. Every inch of the body and all body seams are finished to a level of perfection rarely, if ever, achieved in a factory build.


Tubular steel control arms are mounted on the Detroit Speed front subframe. Coil-over shock suspension units are part of the manufacturer’s suspension package.


Paul Stenquist


The rear axle is mounted on a Detroit Speed 4-link suspension system. Coil-over shocks manage ride-height adjustment and damping. A stout sway bar controls body roll.


Paul Stenquist


The chassis and suspension are completely new and capable of far better handling and traction than the original running gear. The underside of the unibody was fitted with rigid, steel frame connectors that tie the front subframe and rear suspension together, effectively controlling unibody flex. A near-bulletproof 9-inch Ford third member with 3.73:1 cogs hangs on the 4-link rear suspension, with coil-over shocks providing damping and wheel control. The same type of shock and spring units are used up front on a subframe with tubular steel control arms. All chassis and suspension parts are from Detroit Speed. The same manufacturer supplied a mini-tub kit that enables the use of tires worthy of the machine.


Forgeline aluminum wheels are mounted with Continental Sport Plus tires, front and rear. The rears are 295/35/ZR18, and the fronts are 275/35/ZR18. The rear tires have a 10-inch tread width, while the fronts measure 9.4 inches across the tread. That’s big rubber.


While most of this Camaro is an exercise in subtlety, that fat rubber offers an aggressive counterpoint.


Paul Stenquist


Forgeline 18-inch polished aluminum wheels mount Continental Sport Plus 295/35 ZR18 tires in the rear and 275/35 ZR18 tires up front.


Paul Stenquist


The Chevy LT4 crate engine is a 6.2-liter supercharged small-block V-8. GM claims 650 horsepower at 6400 rpm. Torque is 650 lb-ft at 3600 rpm. The block and cylinder heads are aluminum. The lower end utilizes 6-bolt cross-bolted main caps, a forged-steel crank, forged powdered-metal rods, and forged aluminum pistons. An Eaton supercharger delivers over 9 pounds of boost. The static compression ratio is 10:1.


Paul Stenquist


Under the hood, a supercharged LT4 crate motor provides 650 horsepower at 6400 rpm and 650 lb-ft of torque at 3600 rpm. Like most GM crate motors, it came with all necessary wiring and a control unit. It delivers power to GM’s heavy-duty Hydra-Matic 6L90 six-speed automatic transmission. The LT4 engine delivers the same kind of smooth and reliable performance in this 57-year-old car as it did in the[2024 ZL1 Camaro](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/chevrolet/camaro/2024/2024-chevrolet-camaro-zl1?id=aCn8W000000PI5JSAW) .


The interior was made to Young’s specifications in shades of grey. The console includes electronic transmission controls.


Paul Stenquist


Paul Stenquist


Paul Stenquist


Dakota Digital analog gauges mount in the stock-appearing dash. A Vintage A/C system pipes in cool air through Camaro’s original vents.


For me, the most appealing part of this machine is its style. From its well-detailed interior, finished in shades of gray, to exterior flourishes—including flush-fitting glass, body-hugging bumpers, clean flanks, tucked-in tailpipes, near-flawless sheet metal, a silken mirror-like finish, and those bright 18-inch Forgeline wheels—the car delights in a multitude of ways. It’s a moving experience, even while parked in Young’s backyard.


The paint is Hypersonic Grey, a 20 Corvette color. It was applied by Gordie Wilton. The finish is mirror-like.


Paul Stenquist


Note the flush fit of the windshield, bumpers, and door handles. Nothing interrupts the pretty lines of this machine.


Paul Stenquist


While some performance cars shout, “look at me,” Young’s Camaro just sings harmoniously.


Paul Stenquist


The differential is a Ford 9-inch mounted in a narrowed housing. The ratio is 3.73:1.


Paul Stenquist


Erik Stenquist
